headline: Appledore boulders give up cod and haddock, bluefish chew the Piscataqua mouth
subhead: Thirteen miles of coast doesn't need padding when the Shoals structure is loaded and the bunker schools are finally stacking the harbors.
body_markdown:
Every summer somebody from away pulls into the state pier, looks at the chart, and asks where the real fishing is since New Hampshire's coastline barely cracks thirteen miles. That question gets answered the same way every year — point the bow six miles offshore to the Isles of Shoals and fish it like it's a hundred and thirty. The boulder fields off Appledore and White Island don't care how short the coastline is on a map. They fish like Jeffreys Ledge on a good day, and this week they did exactly that for the boats willing to run out early and work the drift right.

The pattern right now is a split one, and it's worth being straight about it. Offshore at the Shoals, the groundfish bite has been steady — not a blitz, but dependable, which this time of year is worth more. Inshore, the striper and bluefish game is still catching up to where it should be for Labor Day week. Bunker haven't fully concentrated in the harbors yet, and that's held the inshore bite to windows instead of all-day action. We flagged this pattern last week, calling for stability through the next several days with the real seasonal turn still a couple weeks out, and that's exactly how it's played. Bluefish activity has tracked bunker density almost point for point — thin bait, thin blitzes; when a pod of pogies pushes into Hampton Harbor or past Rye Harbor's breakwall, the blues show up on them within the tide.

At the Shoals, boats working the rock piles and ledges between Appledore, White Island, and Star Island are finding cod in the 40 to 70 foot range, with the better fish coming off bottom on jigs — diamond jigs and 4 to 6 ounce Norwegian-style jigs tipped with a clam strip — worked on the last of the ebb through the start of the flood, when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a mooring's worth of lead. Haddock are mixed in on the same structure but running smaller on average this month; most of the keeper-sized fish are coming from the deeper humps off White Island in 70 to 90 feet, still on clam belly or squid strips fished on a standard cod rig with a short dropper. Nothing has been what you'd call fast, but a two-to-three hour drift session at the Shoals is putting a mixed box of cod and haddock in the fish hold for boats that know which pieces of bottom hold fish on a given tide stage — the north side pieces fish better on the incoming, the south-facing rock tends to hold fish through the slack.

Mackerel have been schooling thick around the Shoals and pushing up into the mouth of the Piscataqua on the last of the flood, and that's been the saving grace for bait — small Swedish jigs or a mackerel tree worked through the school fills a bucket in minutes, and fresh mackerel strip has been outproducing frozen clam on the groundfish drifts by a wide margin this week.

Inshore, the striper story is patchy but not dead. Hampton Harbor is holding fish on the push — the channel edges near the Route 1A bridge and the deeper cuts by the Willows have given up schoolie-to-mid-slot bass on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets funneled through the inlet against the current. Live pogies under a slip float or a white paddletail swimming plug worked slow along the channel edge has been the better presentation over straight bucktails this week — the bass have been sluggish enough that a slower retrieve is closing more bites than a fast one. Great Boars Head has produced after dark on eels and darters fished tight to the rocks on the outgoing tide, though it's been a game of patience rather than volume. Rye Harbor's breakwall and the rocks off Odiorne Point have both given up bluefish in the 3 to 6 pound class on metal — Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks in chrome — worked through the surface froth when the blues show on bait, which has mostly been dawn and the last hour of daylight.

Flounder season in the harbors is winding down fast as the water starts its slow cool-off, but there are still fish to be had on bloodworms and clam in the deeper channel bends of Hampton Harbor and Rye Harbor on the slower stages of the tide, before the current picks up and blows the rig around.

The moon is building toward full over the next several days, which means more water moving through the inlets and, with it, better odds of bait finally concentrating the way it needs to for a real inshore push. If that bait shows up thick in Hampton Harbor or off Great Boars Head, expect the bluefish to answer within a tide cycle and the striper bite to sharpen behind it. Offshore, there's no reason to expect the Shoals groundfish bite to do anything but hold steady through the coming week — the structure doesn't change, and the fish sitting on it haven't shown any sign of leaving. If there's only one day to fish this week, run to the Shoals early on a dropping tide for the cod and haddock, then swing back inshore on the last of the flood to check Hampton Harbor's channel edges for bass working the bait push. Keep the eel bucket ready for after dark at Boars Head — that bite has been the most consistent thing going this week, small as the window is.
